initial_observation.encounter_context: presented with a sudden temporal relative scotoma in the left eye; had been working with COVID-19 patients during the 5 weeks prior to onset
initial_observation.chief_complaint: sudden temporal relative scotoma in the left eye
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 for the left eye, and no discromatopsy or afferent pupillary defect was present. A visual field test (SITA Fast 30-2) was performed, with no significant findings associated with a focal loss of sensitivity described by the patient. The anterior segment and fundus examination were unremarkable in both eyes.
presenting_symptoms: sudden temporal relative scotoma in the left eye
known_prior_history: no previous retinal disease or systemic disease with retinal compromise
worked with COVID-19 patients during the 5 weeks prior to onset

evidence_items.source_text: Swept-source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT, Topcon Co., Tokyo, Japan) showed a hyperreflective band at the level of ganglion cell and inner plexiform layers, which spared the outer retina (Fig. 1a, b).
Fluorescein angiography showed no areas of leakage or vascular exudation in early or late phases.
Blood tests performed were normal, with no signs of coagulopathy alterations. The patient had normal blood pressure values.
Real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was negative.
ELISA testing and a third rapid antibody detection test performed 7 days after the onset of symptoms were positive.

In the subsequent follow-up of the patient 30 days after the start of the scotoma perception, he continued to describe it. Retinal imaging study showed the same hyperreflective lesions observed in SS-OCT, with even greater intensity (Fig. 2a, b), and there were no arteries or veins in the inner layers of the retina on this B-scan that could cause a hyperreflective shadow.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: ours is a case of COVID-19 diagnosed through an imaging study of the retina.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: After identifying the aforementioned retinal lesions and considering the patient’s high-risk profession with regard to COVID-19 exposure, a pharyngeal swab test for SARS-CoV-2 ribonucleic acid (RNA) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) determination of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) were requested.
Real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) was negative. ELISA testing and a third rapid antibody detection test performed 7 days after the onset of symptoms were positive.

This case, and the papers presented by other authors [5, 6, 11], support the hypothesis that these retinal OCT findings should be considered another sign of COVID-19 disease, hence the importance of retinal imaging study in these patients.
